content.text: Book reference: Chapter 11, pages 345–387. Guided Exercises: Reviewing Syslog Files, Reviewing System Journal Entries, Preserving the System Journal, Maintaining Accurate Time. Lab: Analyzing and Storing Logs.
RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — This whole chapter

journalctl filtering (by priority, time range, and unit) and making the journal persistent across reboot are both standard, hands-on RHCSA tasks — and reading logs correctly is the single most transferable real-world troubleshooting skill in this entire course.

sections.title: 11.1 The logging architecture — two services, two jobs

content.text: Two services split the logging work on RHEL 8, and understanding the division is the key to this whole chapter:
| Service | Job |

| `systemd-journald` | Collects EVERYTHING — kernel messages, early boot output, every daemon's stdout/stderr, and syslog events — restructures them into a standard format, and writes them to the structured, indexed, BINARY journal. By default this lives in /run/log/journal, which does NOT survive a reboot. |
| `rsyslog` | Reads syslog-type messages back out of the journal as they arrive, and sorts them into traditional plain-text files under /var/log, based on rules keyed on facility and priority. |
💡 Why this matters — Why two systems instead of one

journald's binary format is what makes journalctl's fast filtering (by time, priority, unit, PID) possible at all — a plain text file can't be queried that efficiently. rsyslog's plain-text files in /var/log exist for compatibility with the huge ecosystem of tools (grep, tail, log-shipping agents, older scripts) built around simple text logs over decades. You get the query power of one and the universal compatibility of the other, at the cost of the same data effectively existing in two forms.
Key /var/log files
| File | Contents |
| `/var/log/messages` | Most syslog messages — EXCEPT authentication, mail, cron, and pure debug messages, which are split out below |
| `/var/log/secure` | Authentication and security events — this is where failed/successful SSH logins show up |
| `/var/log/maillog` | Mail server activity |
| `/var/log/cron` | Scheduled job (cron) execution |
| `/var/log/boot.log` | Non-syslog console messages from system startup |
NOTE — Not every application logs through rsyslog

Not every application uses syslog — some (like the Apache web server) write their own logs directly, conventionally still somewhere under /var/log, just in their own subdirectory and format rather than through rsyslog's rules.
Syslog priorities — highest to lowest severity
| Code | Priority | Meaning |
| `0` | `emerg` | System is unusable |
| `1` | `alert` | Action must be taken immediately |
| `2` | `crit` | Critical condition |
| `3` | `err` | Non-critical error |
| `4` | `warning` | Warning condition |
| `5` | `notice` | Normal but significant |
| `6` | `info` | Informational |
| `7` | `debug` | Debug-level detail |

rsyslog's rules live in /etc/rsyslog.conf and any *.conf file under /etc/rsyslog.d/. Each rule reads facility.priority destination — e.g. authpriv.* /var/log/secure sends every authpriv-facility message, at any priority, to /var/log/secure. none excludes a facility explicitly (useful when a message would otherwise match more than one rule and get logged twice).

Log rotation: logrotate runs daily via a scheduled job and renames aging files (e.g. /var/log/messages → /var/log/messages-20190130), starting a fresh file and eventually discarding the oldest copies (typically after about 4 weeks) so logs don't consume unbounded disk space.
Reading a syslog line
Feb 11 20:11:48 localhost sshd[1433]: Failed password for student from 172.25.0.10 port 59344 ssh2
| Field | Value in the example |
| Timestamp | Feb 11 20:11:48 |
| Host | localhost |
| Program[PID] | sshd[1433] |
| Message | Failed password for student from 172.25.0.10 port 59344 ssh2 |

tail -f /var/log/secure is the standard way to watch a log live while you reproduce a problem — same technique as monitoring any growing file. logger lets you inject a test message manually (default facility.priority is user.notice unless you set -p explicitly) — genuinely useful for confirming a new rsyslog rule actually fires before you rely on it.
RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — This is the single most tested command in this chapter
journalctl's filtering options (-n, -f, -p, --since/--until, -b, unit filters) are used constantly for the rest of this course and on the exam. Fluency here is disproportionately high-value.
| Command | Shows |
| `journalctl` | Everything in the journal, oldest first, paged through less |
| `journalctl -n 20` | Just the last 20 entries (default is 10 if you omit the number) |
| `journalctl -f` | Live-follow, like tail -f, for new entries as they arrive — Ctrl+C to stop |
| `journalctl -p err` | Entries at err priority OR HIGHER (accepts either the name or number of any of the 8 syslog priorities) |
| `journalctl --since today` | Everything from midnight today onward |
| `journalctl --since "2019-02-10 20:30:00" --until "2019-02-13 12:00:00"` | An explicit date/time range (the quotes are required — they preserve the embedded space) |
| `journalctl --since "-1 hour"` | Relative time — also accepts yesterday/today/tomorrow as shortcuts |
| `journalctl -b` | This boot only |

| `journalctl -b -1` | The PREVIOUS boot — the standard first move when debugging a crash, since the crash's own final messages are usually at the end of the boot before the one you're currently running |
| `journalctl _SYSTEMD_UNIT=sshd.service` | Only entries tied to one specific unit |
| `journalctl _PID=1182` | Only entries from one specific process ID |

Multiple field filters can be combined in one query for a genuinely narrow, fast search — e.g. journalctl _SYSTEMD_UNIT=sshd.service _PID=1182 shows only that one process's sshd activity, filtering out everything else in the journal at once.
💡 Why this matters — Colored output is a built-in triage signal

journalctl bolds notice/warning-priority entries and shows err-or-higher entries in red automatically — scanning for red text in a wall of output is a fast first pass before you reach for -p to filter formally.

journalctl -o verbose reveals every underlying structured field on each entry (_PID, _UID, _COMM, _EXE, _SYSTEMD_UNIT, and more) — any of these can become a filter key in a later query, which is how the unit/PID filters above actually work under the hood.

sections.title: 11.3 Making the journal survive a reboot

content.text: By default the journal lives only in /run/log/journal — part of an in-memory filesystem that's wiped every reboot. Configure persistence in /etc/systemd/journald.conf.
| Storage= value | Effect |
| `volatile` | /run/log/journal only — cleared every reboot (effectively the default behavior) |
| `persistent` | /var/log/journal — survives reboots; systemd-journald creates the directory itself if it doesn't already exist |
| `auto` | Persistent IF /var/log/journal already exists, volatile otherwise — this is the default when Storage= is left unset |
# /etc/systemd/journald.conf:
[Journal]
Storage=persistent
sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald
RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — This is a two-step task, same pattern as Chapter 9

Edit the config file, THEN restart the service — editing alone does nothing until the daemon re-reads it. Confirm with ls /var/log/journal/ (a hex-named subdirectory containing system.journal and per-user *.journal files) after a reboot, not just after the restart.

Even with persistence on, journals aren't kept forever: a built-in rotation triggers monthly, and by default the journal is capped at 10% of its filesystem's total size while always leaving at least 15% free — both tunable in the same config file.
💡 Why this matters — Why this belongs in a logging chapter

Every log entry and journal entry is only as useful as its timestamp. Comparing events across multiple servers — the normal case in any real troubleshooting — is meaningless if their clocks disagree, which is exactly why accurate time sits in the same chapter as log analysis.
timedatectl
Reports local time, UTC, time zone, and whether NTP synchronization is currently active — one command for the full picture.
| Command | Effect |
| `timedatectl list-timezones` | Lists every valid IANA time zone name (Continent/City format) |
| `tzselect` | Interactively helps you find the correct zone name for your location — READ-ONLY, changes nothing on its own |
| `timedatectl set-timezone America/Phoenix` | Actually changes the system's time zone |
| `timedatectl set-time "09:00:00"` | Sets the system clock manually |
| `timedatectl set-ntp true` | Turns NTP synchronization on (in RHEL 8 this controls the chronyd service specifically) |
NOTE — Time zone naming isn't always the obvious city

Names are Continent/City, but the city chosen isn't always the largest in the zone — it's picked to disambiguate regions with different daylight-saving rules. Arizona doesn't observe daylight saving time while most of the US Mountain zone does, so Arizona gets its own America/Phoenix rather than sharing America/Denver.
chronyd — the NTP client that keeps the clock honest

The local hardware clock (RTC) drifts on its own over time. chronyd continuously corrects it against configured NTP servers; if the network is unavailable, it estimates and records the drift instead, in the driftfile named in /etc/chrony.conf.
| Concept | Meaning |

| Stratum | Hop-count from a reference clock. Stratum 0 = the reference itself, stratum 1 = a server directly attached to it, stratum 2 = synced from a stratum-1 server, and so on — lower stratum generally means higher quality/precision. |
| server line | An NTP source one stratum above yours |
| peer line | An NTP source at the SAME stratum as yours (mutual synchronization, not hierarchical) |
| iburst option | Takes several rapid initial measurements right after startup for faster, more accurate initial sync — recommended on every server line |
# /etc/chrony.conf:
server classroom.example.com iburst
sudo systemctl restart chronyd
chronyc sources -v
In chronyc sources output, an asterisk * in the leftmost state column marks the source currently being used for synchronization — the one indicator worth checking first after any config change.

sections.title: Hands-on: practice these on your own lab

content.text: 1. sudo tail -20 /var/log/secure on servera — find a recent SSH login line and identify its timestamp, PID, and message fields.
2. journalctl -p err -b — check for any error-or-higher entries from the current boot.
3. journalctl -u sshd --since "-1 hour" — combine a unit filter with a relative time range in one query.
4. sudo vim /etc/systemd/journald.conf, set Storage=persistent, sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald, then sudo reboot and confirm ls /var/log/journal/ shows a populated directory afterward.
5. timedatectl — note your current time zone and NTP sync status. timedatectl list-timezones | grep America to find your own region's exact name if different.
6. chronyc sources -v — identify which source (if any) shows the * currently-synced marker.
1. Q1 — You need to see only error-or-worse journal entries from the boot before the one the system is currently running. Write the single journalctl command that does this.
2. Q2 — A server was rebooted and journalctl now shows nothing from before the reboot. What's the most likely cause, and the two-step fix?
3. Q3 — Why does comparing timestamps across two servers' logs become meaningless if their clocks have drifted apart, and what service exists specifically to prevent that?
NOTE — Answers
Q1 — journalctl -p err -b -1

Q2 — The journal is almost certainly still on its default volatile storage (/run/log/journal, wiped every boot). Fix: set Storage=persistent in /etc/systemd/journald.conf, then systemctl restart systemd-journald — editing the file alone does nothing until the daemon reloads it.

Q3 — If two servers' clocks disagree, you can't reliably tell which event on server A actually happened before or after an event on server B — the whole point of comparing timestamped logs across systems collapses. chronyd exists to keep every machine's clock synchronized to the same NTP time source, so cross-server timestamp comparison stays meaningful.

- systemd-journald collects everything into a structured binary journal (queryable with journalctl); rsyslog reads syslog-type messages back out and sorts them into traditional plain-text files under /var/log by facility/priority rules in /etc/rsyslog.conf and /etc/rsyslog.d/.
- /var/log/messages, secure, maillog, cron, and boot.log are the key files to know by content; logrotate keeps them from growing unbounded.
- journalctl -n / -f / -p / --since / --until / -b / unit-and-PID filters are the core toolkit — fluency here is disproportionately high-value for the exam and for real troubleshooting.
- The journal is volatile (/run/log/journal, wiped on reboot) unless Storage=persistent is set in /etc/systemd/journald.conf AND systemd-journald is restarted — both steps are required.

- timedatectl manages time zone and clock settings; chronyd (configured in /etc/chrony.conf, checked with chronyc sources) keeps the clock synchronized via NTP — essential for any timestamp comparison across multiple servers.
